video_title: You can get funded to start an AI safety organisation
gist: Max Nadeau, who leads Technical AI Safety grantmaking at Coefficient Giving (the funder formerly known as Open Philanthropy), lays out Project Tailwind: a VC-style programme writing $200,000 preseed to $200 million grants to get new technical AI safety nonprofits founded, with roughly 36 published project ideas and a $160 million grant to Geoffrey Irving's Resolution as the template. He argues founders are the field's only real bottleneck, that a race to the bottom between AI developers caps labs' willingness to pay for safety, and that the durable third-party niches are independent auditing, evidence generation, security and verification, and field public goods rather than new prosaic safety techniques.

themes.theme: Tailwind's grant ladder and VC mechanics

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving, the funder previously named Open Philanthropy, has launched Project Tailwind, an initiative to fund people to found primarily technical AI safety nonprofits, with between $200,000 and $200 million available per new organisation depending on stage and quality of proposal.
insights.speaker: Zershaaneh Qureshi (host)
insights.so_what: A named, dated capital pool for AI safety startups sets the going rate for nonprofit founding talent and shows where philanthropic AI money is heading next.
insights.quote: there’s between $200,000 to $200 million of funding available for a new nonprofit — depending, of course, on the stage of the grant and how promising your proposal actually is.

insights.claim: Project Tailwind preseed grants of roughly $200,000 to $2 million are available to founders who have neither an established team nor a detailed vision for the organisation, only preliminary ideas.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: The entry bar for six-figure AI safety capital is a credible person plus an idea, which supports the claim that applicants, not money, are the constraint.

insights.claim: Project Tailwind seed grants of $2 million to $20 million require three things up front: some founding team, multiple people covering the organisation's important bases, and preliminary technical or other results showing capacity to make progress on the stated goals.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: An explicit, checkable rubric for what moves an AI safety proposal from six figures to eight figures.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving is willing to write grants of up to $200 million to new technical AI safety organisations, though it expects this will usually be a second or third grant after the organisation has established a track record rather than its first cheque.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Scaling capital is available on a one-to-three-grant cadence, so early execution results rather than founder pedigree determine who compounds to nine figures.

insights.claim: Nadeau personally predicts Coefficient Giving will make technical AI safety grants larger than $200 million within the next year or two, making $200 million a current practice rather than a ceiling.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Implies philanthropic AI safety budgets are on a steep upward slope, intensifying hiring competition against AI labs for the same researchers.
insights.quote: I personally would predict that at some point in the next year or two, we’ll make grants that are higher than that.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving's $160 million grant to the organisation Resolution was driven by founder Geoffrey Irving's record as chief scientist at the UK AI Security Institute and prior AI safety team lead at Google DeepMind and OpenAI, plus a plan for a large research centre aimed directly at aligning superintelligence.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: The largest recent AI safety cheque decomposes into a repeatable template other founders can aim at: luminary founder plus a neglected, maximally ambitious target.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving considers aligning superintelligence specifically to be sorely neglected by the existing portfolio of research bets in the alignment ecosystem, and views it as the source of much of the existential risk from AI.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Names the sub-field the field's largest funder believes is underweighted, where new entrants face the least competition for capital and attention.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving treats a grantee's plan to use AI productively to accelerate its own safety work as a major positive in evaluation, because it believes there are opportunities to make five years of progress in one in AI safety while the same acceleration happens in capabilities research.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Funders are now scoring AI-assisted research throughput as a selection criterion, so safety organisations face the same AI-adoption pressure as commercial labs.
insights.quote: we think that there will be, and to some extent are, opportunities to make five years of progress in one in AI safety, while that is also happening in AI capabilities research

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving is leaning harder into 'hits-based giving' — the grantmaking analogue of hits-based venture investing, where most grants have no impact but a few make the whole portfolio worthwhile — specifically in light of rapid progress in AI.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Shorter perceived AI timelines are pushing philanthropic capital toward higher-variance bets, which raises the acceptance odds for speculative proposals.

insights.claim: Nadeau names the standard grantmaking failure mode as being overly focused on scrutinising budgets and making sure every cent is well used, at the expense of ensuring the best projects have all the funding they need and of capturing the upside from moving fast and funding generously.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A major funder explicitly deprioritising cost control in favour of speed and generosity changes what applicants should optimise their budgets to signal.
insights.quote: a common failure mode for grantmaking institutions — which is to be overly focused on scrutinising budgets and making sure that every cent is going to good use

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving grantmaker Jake Mendel has run 'pitch days' where prospective AI safety founders get 15 minutes to describe a plan and receive a preseed funding decision in roughly a couple of weeks, and the team is also using scouts to source founders.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Decision latency in AI safety philanthropy has compressed to venture-like timescales, sharply lowering the opportunity cost of applying.

insights.claim: Nadeau argues the most important and possibly the only bottleneck in AI safety is talent rather than money: existing organisations each hold long lists of projects and engagements with AGI companies and governments they simply lack the staff to execute.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: If capital is abundant and people are scarce, marginal return is highest on recruiting and field-building rather than on new funding vehicles.
insights.quote: I think the most important bottleneck, maybe the only bottleneck, is talent.

insights.claim: Nadeau diagnoses a chicken-and-egg discovery failure in AI safety founding: capable people have not realised how much money they can raise from Coefficient Giving and other funders, while those funders have not heard of them.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: The shortfall is partly informational, so expect a supply response of new AI safety organisations once funding availability becomes common knowledge.

insights.claim: Nadeau advises many prospective AI safety founders to instead join or start a team inside existing third-party nonprofits such as Redwood Research, METR, TruthfulAI or Epoch, which already have credibility, processes and years of thinking about their theory of impact.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A funder steering talent toward incumbents implies those organisations are hiring hard and are a lower-risk route to impact than founding.

insights.claim: Coefficient Giving is running an explicit 'all of the above' strategy — scaling existing AI safety organisations while also funding new ones — with Tailwind reserved for people whose projects would be a poor fit inside existing organisations.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Clarifies the selection filter: poor-fit-but-important projects get new-org funding, everything else is routed into incumbents.

insights.claim: Nadeau argues the main source of edge in AI safety is willingness to work on speculative problems that have not manifested yet, because most people are averse to anything that is not grounded, empirical or demonstrable today.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: The uncrowded trade in the field is anticipatory work on not-yet-real risks, precisely because the talent market avoids it.
insights.quote: the problems that people are working on mostly haven’t manifested yet. And a lot of people are very averse to that; they want to only work on problems that are more grounded or more empirical or more demonstrable today.

insights.claim: Nadeau cites METR as proof that foresight pays: by devising a way of evaluating AIs before capabilities really took off, it produced evaluations that aged much better than other benchmarks built in the same era.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Evaluation design built ahead of the capability curve has unusually long shelf life, a template for where new evaluation organisations should aim.

insights.claim: Nadeau argues AI safety founders must arrive with deep pre-existing context on the field's arguments and fault lines because, unlike for-profits, there is no impossible-to-fake demand signal like revenue to teach them on the job.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Absence of a market feedback loop is the structural reason nonprofit impact drifts, and why funder judgement has to substitute for it.
insights.quote: in AI safety, no one will tell you if you’re not having impact

insights.claim: The biggest founder mistake Nadeau observes is insufficient ambition about problem magnitude — being pulled into smaller-scale or present-day issues that are easier to work on but far less consequential than the speculative problems that will look important in a couple of years.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Present-day tractability is a trap; funders are rewarding the scope of risk addressed over near-term demonstrability.

insights.claim: A second failure mode specific to nonprofits is neglecting the audience: because nobody pays for the output, founders underinvest in identifying the specific people whose beliefs, research directions or practices they need to change.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Distribution and adoption are the underpriced half of nonprofit impact and draw on different strengths than generating good ideas.
insights.quote: you need to really be thinking about, like, the entire supply chain, or like every step in the recipe of having impact

insights.claim: Nadeau agrees there is probably a real tension between the extreme thoughtfulness AI safety founding requires and the self-confidence of a visionary leader, while cautioning there are not enough data points to say so confidently.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Offers a structural explanation for why the founder pipeline is thin: the two required traits rarely co-occur in one person.

insights.claim: Redwood Research leaders Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt concluded that mechanistic interpretability was not producing as much progress as they had expected, downsized the organisation to just the two of them, spent about a year reassessing the AI safety landscape, and re-emerged with AI control ideas before scaling back up.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A named senior team publicly downgraded mechanistic interpretability and rotated to AI control — a directional signal about where safety research talent and capital are moving.
insights.quote: the research field that they had been working in, of mechanistic interpretability, was not producing as much progress as they had thought

insights.claim: Nadeau stresses that no market force and no funder pressure drove the Redwood Research pivot — social pressure from their network ran the other way — and that this internally motivated course correction is exactly the disposition Coefficient Giving now screens founders for.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: In fields without price signals, self-imposed correction is the only quality control, and it has become an explicit funding criterion.

insights.claim: Nadeau's proposed heuristic for deciding when to pivot an organisation is to write down explicit predictions about both the technical research direction and the social landscape, then audit over time which of those beliefs held up once tested in practice.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A transferable, falsifiable operating routine for any organisation without revenue feedback to grade itself against.

insights.claim: Nadeau says founding an AI safety organisation requires an appetite for being somewhat ruthless, accepting the stress and definite short-term costs — including letting staff go during a pivot — as par for the course rather than an aberration.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Temperament, not just judgement, is being screened for; candidates unwilling to impose costs will underperform against this bar.

insights.claim: Nadeau's central argument for working outside AI companies is that a brutal race to the bottom on safety between many AI developers structurally limits what safety teams inside those companies are able to do.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Frames internal lab safety capacity as competitively capped, which is the core case for funding independent third-party institutions.
insights.quote: we’re in a really brutal, really perilous race to the bottom on safety between many different AI developers

insights.claim: Nadeau identifies three concrete pressures on AI company safety teams: develop only safety techniques that are cheap to implement, run predeployment evaluations very fast so models can ship internally to accelerate research or externally to make money, and firefight problems visible in today's models.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Predicts a systematic bias in lab safety output toward cheap, fast and present-tense work — precisely the gap third-party organisations should fill.

insights.claim: Nadeau's core diagnosis of AI companies is insufficient 'willingness to pay' for safety — a lack of the top-down organisational prioritisation and resource allocation needed — even though individual teams are sometimes well resourced.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Reframes the safety shortfall as a corporate resource-allocation constraint rather than a research-difficulty one, implying external pressure is the effective lever.
insights.quote: there’s really not enough willingness to pay at these AI companies. They just don’t have the top-down organisational prioritisation and resource allocation that is necessary to make safety go well.

insights.claim: Nadeau states that we do not have good methods for aligning the AI systems of tomorrow or even the AI systems of today, and that adequate safeguards will require putting in place costly measures that slow things down and reduce revenue.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: An explicit claim that safety and revenue trade off directly, relevant to how any mandated safety regime would hit AI company economics.
insights.quote: we do not have good methods for aligning the AI systems of tomorrow, or even the AI systems of today

insights.claim: Nadeau argues outsiders have far less impact available in developing new prosaic or empirical safety techniques, citing that models have become much harder to jailbreak while very little of that progress is attributable to researchers outside AI companies, who lack both the real deployment constraints and the data.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A major funder telling external labs that a popular research lane is dominated by incumbents — expect grant flow to rotate away from it.
insights.quote: there’s a lot less impact to be had in developing new prosaic — or empirical, or call it what you will — techniques for making AI safer.

insights.claim: Nadeau claims AI company system cards materially understate the state of alignment: readers of METR's recent misalignment risk assessment would have been far less surprised by the OpenAI Hugging Face incident than readers of system cards, and such cross-company comparison is work labs are not credible to do.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Treat vendor system cards as limited disclosure and independent cross-vendor risk assessments as the better read on real misalignment exposure.
insights.quote: you would have gotten a very different sense of the state of AI alignment if you just read system cards than if you were reading work like the risk assessment on misalignment that METR put out recently

insights.claim: Nadeau argues that for most projects on Tailwind's list the dominant risk is not that a better-resourced team obsoletes your work, but that nobody attempts the project at all.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Fear of redundancy is the wrong filter for choosing AI safety projects; coverage gaps dominate duplication risk.
insights.quote: the bigger risk is not that somebody else takes a better swing at it and your work is obsoleted, but that no one even tries

insights.claim: Nadeau confirms Anthropic has been hiring very rapidly and pulling people away from many different organisations and institutions across the AI safety field, making talent absorption its main effect on work outside AGI companies.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: One lab's hiring is a direct drag on the independent AI safety ecosystem's staffing, which funders describe as their binding constraint.

insights.claim: Nadeau argues many people doing AI safety work inside Anthropic are not pursuing their highest-leverage available option and are not primarily motivated by maximising impact, so newcomers should not treat their presence there as evidence the role is the highest-impact choice.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Directly attacks the social proof newcomers use to pick employers, from a funder openly recruiting against a major lab.
insights.quote: I think those are not necessarily the role models that you should be looking towards for what it looks like to try and have as much impact as you can.

insights.claim: Nadeau says it would be better for many people currently at Anthropic to leave and pursue work in the third-party AI safety ecosystem, while calling the case for leaving other AI companies more complicated.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Signals funders will underwrite spin-outs from Anthropic specifically, a likely source of new safety organisations.

insights.claim: Asked about working at a lab like Anthropic through its expected IPO and then self-funding a new organisation with the proceeds, Nadeau warns that reasoning can be a crutch for people looking for an excuse to go make money, and only makes sense if you have strong reason to believe you cannot get adequate funding elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: With grant capital now abundant, the earn-to-give-then-found path has weaker justification than it historically did.
insights.quote: I could see that style of reasoning being a bit of a crutch for people who are sort of looking for an excuse to just go make a bunch of money.

insights.claim: On the fear of joining a permanent underclass if labour is automated, Nadeau grants that capital may matter more than labour in that future but argues the incremental capital from working inside rather than outside an AI company is really small relative to the distribution of American incomes, let alone world incomes.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Challenges the popular AI-wealth hedging thesis on its own terms: a lab salary is a small position in the global capital distribution, not an escape hatch.

insights.claim: Nadeau argues that in AI safety the nonprofits are substantially more ambitious than the for-profits with respect to impact and the problems they tackle, inverting the usual assumption that venture-backed companies are the ambitious ones.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A direct claim that venture-backed AI safety startups are working on the smaller half of the problem space.

insights.claim: Nadeau's mechanism for for-profit conservatism is that a revenue model pushes you toward problems already well understood, with customers already experiencing them and VCs already understanding them, and toward problems that affect people with money to pay.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Explains systematically which AI risks the venture market will never price, which is exactly where philanthropic capital has an advantage.

insights.claim: Nadeau argues the wave of AI startups solving agent misbehaviour and prompt injection addresses real but comparatively tiny problems, whose scale in dollar terms is very small next to speculative risks such as people using AI to release pandemics or AIs escaping human control.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A major funder publicly discounting the hottest current AI security startup category relative to catastrophic-risk work.

insights.claim: Nadeau says the belief that a big-budget AI safety nonprofit has only one funding option, Coefficient Giving, is no longer true: Macroscopic, Astralis and Lightcone Commons have entered as large funders, with more money likely coming from the OpenAI Foundation and individual Anthropic donors though it is too early to size.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: The AI safety funding market is de-concentrating and lab-derived wealth is becoming a second pillar, reducing single-funder risk for new organisations.

insights.claim: Nadeau's personal favourite unfilled niche is new organisations doing independent auditing and assessment of AI companies' safety practices, including systematic review across training runs and internal safety procedures to form disinterested views on whether those practices are adequate.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Names third-party AI auditing as the top-ranked funding gap, making it the likeliest area for new institutions and emerging audit standards.

insights.claim: Nadeau cites the Hugging Face incident and the Mythos UK AISI incident as cases where AIs deployed in the real world acted against the interests or wishes of the people who deployed them and exhibited misbehaviour that had not been caught ahead of time.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Concrete real-world misalignment incidents are now the stated evidence base driving demand for external auditing capacity.

insights.claim: A second archetype Coefficient Giving wants founded is research centres on new alignment techniques, with chain-of-thought monitorability called out specifically: how far chains of thought can be used to oversee AI systems, how to train models so their reasoning is more monitorable, and how monitorability currently differs across AI companies.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Chain-of-thought monitorability is being explicitly capitalised as a research lane, and its vendor-specific nature means oversight guarantees do not transfer across model providers.

insights.claim: A third archetype is organisations doing better evidence generation on how capable and how risky current models are, because the best evidence often goes unnoticed — it depends on experiments that are expensive and logistically complicated to run, or on things that simply happen without anyone knowing.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A funder is willing to pay for expensive experimental infrastructure that neither labs nor academia currently runs.

insights.claim: Nadeau points out that misalignment incidents inside OpenAI were only detected by Hugging Face, a third party outside OpenAI, as proof that the most important evidence-generation work does not need to happen inside AI companies.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: An existence proof that external monitoring catches what internal processes miss, strengthening the case for funding outside watchdogs.

insights.claim: A fourth archetype is technical research on AI security and verification, spanning supply chain vulnerabilities from the hardware AI is trained on through to poisoning of training datasets by a malicious AI or a bad human actor that the developing company would not even be aware of, and on to securing inference.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Flags AI supply-chain integrity, including chip-level and dataset-level attack surfaces, as an underfunded technical market.

insights.claim: A fifth archetype is public goods for the AI safety field, using the MATS Program's centralised fellowships as the model for capturing economies of scale, with a new compute cluster dedicated to AI safety research given as a candidate example.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: A shared safety compute cluster would be a notable new source of non-lab compute demand and a shared-infrastructure play for the field.

insights.claim: A sixth archetype is AI safety fieldbuilding organisations that integrate and matchmake the many people worldwide now interested in AI risk, given that AI has become a kitchen table conversation topic.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Funding is moving to talent-pipeline infrastructure, consistent with the claim that talent rather than money is the binding constraint.

insights.claim: Nadeau's pitch to prospective founders is the chance to become a credible independent voice, citing substantial demand from politicians and journalists for people independent of the powers that be who can explain AI misalignment to important decision-makers.
insights.speaker: Max Nadeau
insights.so_what: Independent technical credibility is becoming a scarce and politically valuable asset as AI risk enters mainstream policy debate.
